name: Ochre pigment
desc: Iron-oxide earth ground and mixed into paint, the oldest known processed pigment.

name: Birch tar adhesive
desc: Adhesive distilled from birch bark by Neanderthals, the earliest known synthetic material.

name: Leather tanning
desc: Treating hides with tannins or minerals to make durable, rot-resistant leather.

name: Native copper working
desc: Hammering naturally occurring metallic copper into beads and tools, the first use of metal.

name: Annealing
desc: Heating work-hardened metal to restore its ductility so it can be shaped further.

name: Lead smelting
desc: Reducing lead ore with fire, probably the first metal extracted from ore.

name: Crucible
desc: Heat-resistant ceramic vessel for melting metals, essential to casting and later crucible steel.

name: Metal casting
desc: Pouring molten metal into moulds to make shaped objects in one step.

name: Gold working
desc: Hammering, casting and joining gold, seen in the Varna necropolis hoard.

name: Arsenical bronze
desc: Copper alloyed with arsenic, the first widely used bronze before tin bronze.

name: Lost-wax casting
desc: Casting from a wax model invested in clay, allowing intricate metal shapes.

name: Bellows
desc: Device forcing air into a furnace to raise its temperature for smelting and forging.

name: Tin
desc: Extraction of tin from cassiterite, the key alloying metal for tin bronze.

name: Cupellation
desc: Refining silver and gold by oxidizing lead in a porous cupel, the basis of silver production.

name: Gilding
desc: Applying thin layers of gold to surfaces, later by fire-gilding with mercury amalgam.

name: Brass
desc: Copper-zinc alloy made first by cementation with zinc ore, later from metallic zinc.

name: Zinc smelting
desc: Distilling metallic zinc from ore in retorts, first done at scale at Zawar in India.

name: Patio process
desc: Mercury amalgamation of silver ore in New Spain, which drove colonial silver output.

name: Faience
desc: Glazed quartz ceramic from Mesopotamia and Egypt, a precursor to true glass.

name: Ceramic glaze
desc: Glassy coating fused onto pottery to make it waterproof and decorative.

name: Egyptian blue
desc: Calcium copper silicate, the first synthetic pigment.

name: Stoneware
desc: Dense, vitrified pottery fired at high temperature, first made in China.

name: Dragon kiln
desc: Long sloping Chinese climbing kiln reaching the high temperatures needed for stoneware and porcelain.

name: Porcelain
desc: Translucent, hard ceramic of kaolin fired above 1200 C, developed in Han China.

name: Tin-glazed pottery
desc: Opaque white tin-oxide glaze from Abbasid Iraq, the basis of maiolica and delftware.

name: European hard-paste porcelain
desc: First European hard-paste porcelain, reverse engineered at Meissen in Saxony.

name: Fire brick
desc: Refractory brick able to line furnaces, critical for high-temperature metallurgy.

name: Glassblowing
desc: Inflating molten glass on a blowpipe, which made glass vessels cheap and common.

name: Crown glass
desc: Window glass made by spinning a blown bubble into a flat disc.

name: Venetian cristallo
desc: Clear, colourless Venetian glass that set Europe's standard for fine glassware.

name: Lead crystal
desc: Ravenscroft's lead-oxide glass, brilliant and dense, later vital for optical flint glass.

name: Plate glass
desc: Cast and polished flat glass for large mirrors and windows, made at Saint-Gobain.

name: Tempered glass
desc: Glass toughened by rapid cooling of its surface, shattering into blunt pieces.

name: Borosilicate glass
desc: Schott's low-expansion glass resistant to thermal shock, used for labware and cookware.

name: Laminated glass
desc: Glass bonded to a plastic interlayer so it holds together when broken.

name: Glass fiber
desc: Fine glass filaments produced in bulk, used for insulation and composites.

name: Glass-ceramic
desc: Glass crystallized under control into a tough ceramic, discovered by Stookey at Corning.

name: Float glass
desc: Pilkington process floating molten glass on molten tin to make flat sheets cheaply.

name: Chemically strengthened glass
desc: Glass toughened by ion exchange that swaps sodium for larger potassium ions.

name: Gorilla Glass
desc: Corning's ion-exchanged aluminosilicate cover glass used on most touchscreen phones.

name: Verneuil process
desc: Flame fusion process making synthetic ruby and sapphire, the first commercial crystal growth.

name: Bloomery
desc: Furnace reducing iron ore below its melting point to a spongy bloom of iron and slag.

name: Wrought iron
desc: Low-carbon iron worked by hammering, the main structural iron until the 1860s.

name: Quenching
desc: Rapid cooling of hot steel in water or oil to harden it.

name: Tempering
desc: Reheating hardened steel to trade some hardness for toughness.

name: Pattern welding
desc: Forge-welding twisted bars of iron and steel into tough, patterned blades.

name: Crucible steel
desc: Steel melted in sealed crucibles, giving uniform high-carbon steel.

name: Wootz steel
desc: High-carbon crucible steel from South India, exported as ingots across Asia.

name: Damascus steel
desc: Blades forged from wootz ingots, famed for their watery pattern and sharpness.

name: Finery forge
desc: Decarburizing cast pig iron into wrought iron, first in Han China then medieval Europe.

name: Tatara furnace
desc: Japanese clay bloomery producing tamahagane steel for swords.

name: Cementation process
desc: Packing wrought iron bars in charcoal to absorb carbon, producing blister steel.

name: Reverberatory furnace
desc: Furnace keeping fuel apart from the charge, allowing coal to be used for smelting.

name: Rolling mill
desc: Passing metal between rollers to make sheet, bar and rail.

name: Tinplate
desc: Rolled iron sheet coated with tin, later the material of food cans.

name: Huntsman crucible steel
desc: Huntsman's Sheffield process of melting blister steel in crucibles for uniform tool steel.

name: Puddling
desc: Cort's process stirring molten pig iron in a coal-fired furnace to make wrought iron at scale.

name: Hot blast
desc: Neilson's preheated air blast that cut blast-furnace fuel use sharply.

name: Ferroalloys
desc: Iron alloys of manganese, silicon or chromium added to control steel chemistry.

name: Metallography
desc: Sorby's microscopic study of polished, etched metal that founded physical metallurgy.

name: Open-hearth furnace
desc: Siemens–Martin regenerative furnace that made most of the world's steel until the 1960s.

name: Tool steel
desc: Mushet's self-hardening tungsten steel for cutting tools.

name: Basic Bessemer process
desc: Thomas and Gilchrist's basic lining that removed phosphorus, opening Europe's phosphoric ores.

name: Manganese steel
desc: Hadfield's tough, work-hardening steel, the first true alloy steel.

name: High-speed steel
desc: Taylor and White's heat-treated tool steel that cut metal several times faster.

name: Electric arc furnace
desc: Héroult's furnace melting steel with electric arcs, now the main route for recycled steel.

name: Electrical steel
desc: Silicon steel with low magnetic losses, used in transformer and motor cores.

name: Induction furnace
desc: Furnace heating metal by induced currents, giving clean melts for alloys.

name: Stainless steel
desc: Chromium steel that resists rust, developed by Brearley and Krupp.

name: Ductile iron
desc: Cast iron with nodular graphite from magnesium additions, strong and tough.

name: Air separation
desc: Linde's cryogenic distillation of air into oxygen and nitrogen on an industrial scale.

name: Continuous casting
desc: Solidifying molten steel directly into slabs and billets, replacing ingot casting.

name: Basic oxygen steelmaking
desc: Linz-Donawitz process blowing pure oxygen into pig iron, the dominant steelmaking route.

name: Direct reduced iron
desc: Reducing iron ore with natural-gas-derived gas below melting, bypassing the blast furnace.

name: Hydrogen-based steelmaking
desc: Swedish fossil-free route reducing iron ore with green hydrogen, first delivered in 2021.

name: Dislocation theory
desc: Taylor, Orowan and Polanyi's explanation of plastic deformation by line defects in crystals.

name: Electroplating
desc: Depositing a metal coating by electric current, first done by Brugnatelli.

name: Powder metallurgy
desc: Shaping metal from compacted, sintered powder, first used by Wollaston for platinum.

name: Hot-dip galvanization
desc: Coating iron with molten zinc to protect it from rust.

name: Gold cyanidation
desc: Leaching gold from low-grade ore with cyanide, still the main gold extraction method.

name: Bayer process
desc: Refining bauxite into alumina, the feedstock for aluminium smelting.

name: Froth flotation
desc: Separating ore minerals by attaching them to air bubbles, enabling low-grade copper mining.

name: Duralumin
desc: Wilm's age-hardening aluminium-copper alloy, the structural metal of airships and aircraft.

name: Ductile tungsten
desc: Coolidge's process making tungsten drawable into wire, used for lamp filaments.

name: Magnesium alloy
desc: Lightest structural metals, developed in Germany as Elektron alloys.

name: Cemented carbide
desc: Tungsten carbide bonded with cobalt, the standard material for cutting tools.

name: Alnico
desc: Aluminium-nickel-cobalt permanent magnet alloy, far stronger than magnet steel.

name: Kroll process
desc: Reducing titanium tetrachloride with magnesium, the basis of all titanium production.

name: Superalloy
desc: Nickel-based alloys like Nimonic that keep their strength in jet engine turbines.

name: Titanium alloys
desc: Light, strong, corrosion-resistant alloys such as Ti-6Al-4V for aircraft and implants.

name: Vacuum arc remelting
desc: Remelting reactive alloys under vacuum to remove gases and inclusions.

name: Metallic glass
desc: Metal alloys cooled so fast they solidify without crystal structure.

name: Shape-memory alloy
desc: Alloys like Nitinol that return to a set shape when heated.

name: Single-crystal turbine blades
desc: Casting superalloy blades as columnar or single crystals to resist creep.

name: Samarium–cobalt magnet
desc: First rare-earth permanent magnet, strong and stable at high temperature.

name: Thermal barrier coating
desc: Ceramic zirconia coatings letting turbine blades run above their melting point.

name: Neodymium magnet
desc: NdFeB magnets, the strongest permanent magnets, used in motors, drives and wind turbines.

name: High-entropy alloy
desc: Alloys of five or more elements in near-equal proportions with unusual properties.

name: Indigo dye
desc: Blue dye from fermented Indigofera leaves, used from ancient Peru to India.

name: Mordant dyeing
desc: Fixing dyes to fibre with metal salts like alum, essential to madder and other dyes.

name: Tyrian purple
desc: Costly Phoenician dye from murex snails, a mark of royalty.

name: Lead white
desc: Basic lead carbonate, the principal white paint pigment until the 20th century.

name: Oil paint
desc: Pigment bound in drying oil, used in Bamiyan and perfected in 15th-century Flanders.

name: Nitric acid
desc: Aqua fortis made by distilling saltpetre with vitriol, used to part gold and silver.

name: Prussian blue
desc: First modern synthetic pigment, discovered by accident in Berlin.

name: Lead chamber process
desc: Roebuck's large-scale sulfuric acid process in lead-lined chambers.

name: Chlorine bleach
desc: Berthollet's chlorine bleaching, later Tennant's bleaching powder, for the textile industry.

name: Leblanc process
desc: Making soda ash from salt and sulfuric acid, the first heavy-chemical industry.

name: Coal tar
desc: Byproduct of coal gas and coke making, the feedstock of the synthetic dye industry.

name: Wöhler synthesis
desc: Synthesis of urea from inorganic salts, launching organic synthesis.

name: Catalysis
desc: Berzelius's recognition that some substances speed reactions without being consumed.

name: Mauveine
desc: Perkin's aniline purple, the first commercial synthetic dye.

name: Solvay process
desc: Ammonia-soda process that displaced Leblanc as the source of sodium carbonate.

name: Azo dyes
desc: Large family of synthetic dyes from diazo coupling, still the most used dye class.

name: Synthetic alizarin
desc: Graebe and Liebermann's synthesis of madder red, which wiped out madder farming.

name: Contact process
desc: Catalytic oxidation of sulfur dioxide giving concentrated sulfuric acid.

name: Synthetic indigo
desc: Laboratory synthesis of indigo that, via BASF in 1897, replaced natural indigo.

name: Chloralkali process
desc: Electrolysis of brine into chlorine and caustic soda, backbone of the chemical industry.

name: Calcium carbide
desc: Willson's electric-furnace product yielding acetylene for lighting and synthesis.

name: Silicon carbide
desc: Acheson's carborundum, a hard synthetic abrasive and later a power semiconductor.

name: Synthetic graphite
desc: Acheson's electric-furnace graphite for electrodes and later nuclear moderators.

name: Ostwald process
desc: Catalytic oxidation of ammonia to nitric acid for fertilizer and explosives.

name: Titanium dioxide pigment
desc: Bright, non-toxic white pigment that replaced lead white in paint.

name: Chlorofluorocarbons
desc: Midgley's Freon refrigerants, later banned for destroying the ozone layer.

name: Nitrocellulose
desc: Schönbein's guncotton, a powerful explosive and the first semi-synthetic polymer.

name: Nitroglycerin
desc: Sobrero's highly sensitive liquid explosive.

name: Blasting cap
desc: Nobel's mercury fulminate detonator, making high explosives usable.

name: Dynamite
desc: Nobel's nitroglycerin absorbed in kieselguhr, safe enough for mining and tunnelling.

name: Smokeless powder
desc: Vieille's Poudre B propellant that replaced black powder in firearms.

name: Picric acid
desc: Phenol-derived high explosive used as lyddite and melinite in shells.

name: Cordite
desc: British double-base smokeless propellant.

name: TNT
desc: Trinitrotoluene, a stable, meltable military explosive mass-produced from 1891.

name: RDX
desc: Cyclonite, a high-brisance explosive central to WWII munitions and plastic explosives.

name: Plastic explosive
desc: Mouldable explosives such as Composition C based on RDX.

name: ANFO
desc: Ammonium nitrate and fuel oil, the cheap bulk explosive of modern mining.

name: Natural rubber
desc: Latex from rubber trees, processed by Mesoamericans to make balls and waterproofing.

name: Gutta-percha
desc: Natural latex that insulated the first submarine telegraph cables.

name: Celluloid
desc: Nitrocellulose plastic first made as Parkesine in 1856, later camphor-plasticized celluloid for film and billiard balls.

name: Rayon
desc: Regenerated cellulose fibre, the first manufactured textile fibre.

name: Cellophane
desc: Transparent regenerated cellulose film, the first clear packaging film.

name: Synthetic rubber
desc: Hofmann's methyl rubber and later Buna, made from small-molecule monomers.

name: Macromolecular theory
desc: Staudinger's proof that polymers are long covalent chains, founding polymer science.

name: Thermal cracking
desc: Burton process breaking heavy oil into gasoline using heat and pressure.

name: Bergius process
desc: Hydrogenating coal into liquid fuels under high pressure.

name: Steam cracking
desc: Cracking hydrocarbons with steam to produce ethylene and propylene, the plastics feedstock.

name: Petrochemicals
desc: Chemicals made from petroleum and gas, starting with isopropanol in 1920.

name: Fischer–Tropsch process
desc: Catalytic conversion of coal-derived syngas into liquid hydrocarbons.

name: PVC
desc: Semon's plasticized polyvinyl chloride, now the third most produced plastic.

name: Neoprene
desc: DuPont's oil-resistant polychloroprene, the first mass-produced synthetic rubber.

name: Styrene-butadiene rubber
desc: Buna S copolymer that became the main tyre rubber after WWII.

name: Polystyrene
desc: Rigid, clear plastic from IG Farben, later foamed as Styrofoam.

name: Aerogel
desc: Kistler's ultralight solid made by replacing a gel's liquid with gas.

name: Polyethylene
desc: ICI's high-pressure polymer of ethylene, crucial for radar cables and now the top plastic.

name: Acrylic glass
desc: Plexiglas, a clear shatter-resistant substitute for glass.

name: Nylon
desc: Carothers's polyamide, the first fully synthetic fibre.

name: Epoxy
desc: Thermosetting resins used as strong adhesives and composite matrices.

name: Polyurethane
desc: Bayer's versatile polymer used for foams, coatings and elastomers.

name: PTFE
desc: Plunkett's Teflon, chemically inert and extremely slippery.

name: Silicone
desc: Silicon-oxygen polymers stable over wide temperatures, made via Rochow's direct process.

name: Polyester (PET)
desc: Whinfield and Dickson's polyester, used in fibres and later drink bottles.

name: Acrylic fiber
desc: Polyacrylonitrile fibre, also the precursor for most carbon fibre.

name: Fluid catalytic cracking
desc: Cracking oil over fluidized catalyst, the main way gasoline is made.

name: Fiberglass
desc: Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic used for boats, car bodies and panels.

name: Synthetic zeolites
desc: Microporous aluminosilicates used as molecular sieves and cracking catalysts.

name: Catalytic reforming
desc: UOP Platforming converting naphtha into high-octane gasoline and aromatics.

name: Ziegler–Natta catalyst
desc: Catalysts polymerizing olefins at low pressure into linear, stereoregular chains.

name: Polycarbonate
desc: Tough transparent thermoplastic used for lenses, discs and glazing.

name: Polypropylene
desc: Natta's isotactic polymer, now the second most produced plastic.

name: Kevlar
desc: Kwolek's para-aramid fibre, five times stronger than steel by weight.

name: UHMWPE fiber
desc: Gel-spun polyethylene fibre (Dyneema), among the strongest fibres per weight.

name: Conductive polymer
desc: Doped polyacetylene showing metallic conductivity, enabling organic electronics.

name: Polylactic acid
desc: Bio-based, compostable polyester made from fermented plant sugar.

name: Carbon fiber
desc: Strong, stiff graphitic filaments, made from PAN at the RAE from 1963.

name: Carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer
desc: Lightweight composite used in aircraft, racing cars and wind blades.

name: Reinforced carbon–carbon
desc: Carbon fibre in a graphite matrix, used on Space Shuttle leading edges and brakes.

name: Ceramic matrix composite
desc: Fibre-toughened ceramics now used in hot sections of jet engines.

name: Synthetic diamond
desc: GE's high-pressure, high-temperature diamond, used as an industrial abrasive.

name: Fullerene
desc: Buckminsterfullerene C60, a new form of carbon found in laser-vaporized graphite.

name: Carbon nanotube
desc: Rolled graphene cylinders with extreme strength and conductivity, reported by Iijima.

name: Graphene
desc: Single atomic layer of carbon isolated by Geim and Novoselov.

name: Twisted bilayer graphene
desc: Graphene layers at a magic angle, showing superconductivity and correlated states.

name: Liquid crystal
desc: Reinitzer's discovery of a phase between liquid and solid, later used in displays.

name: Cyanobiphenyl liquid crystals
desc: Gray's stable room-temperature liquid crystals that made LCDs practical.

name: Czochralski method
desc: Pulling a single crystal from a melt, now used for nearly all silicon wafers.

name: Liquid helium
desc: Kamerlingh Onnes's liquefaction of helium, opening the study of near-absolute-zero matter.

name: Superconductivity
desc: Discovery that mercury loses all electrical resistance below 4.2 K.

name: Niobium–titanium
desc: Ductile superconducting alloy used in MRI magnets and particle accelerators.

name: High-temperature superconductivity
desc: Bednorz and Müller's cuprate superconductors, operating far above previous limits.

name: YBCO
desc: First superconductor working above liquid nitrogen temperature.

name: Iron-based superconductor
desc: Second family of high-temperature superconductors, based on iron pnictides.

name: Barium titanate
desc: Ferroelectric perovskite ceramic, the basis of ceramic capacitors and piezo devices.

name: Lead zirconate titanate
desc: PZT piezoelectric ceramic used in sensors, actuators and ultrasound.

name: Zone refining
desc: Pfann's method of sweeping a molten zone to purify germanium and silicon to parts per billion.

name: Monocrystalline silicon
desc: Single-crystal silicon of electronic grade, the substrate of modern chips.

name: Polysilicon (Siemens process)
desc: Ultrapure silicon deposited from trichlorosilane, feedstock for wafers and solar cells.

name: Gallium arsenide
desc: III-V compound semiconductor for fast transistors, LEDs, lasers and space solar cells.

name: Indium tin oxide
desc: Transparent conductor used in touchscreens and flat-panel displays.

name: Molecular-beam epitaxy
desc: Growing crystal films atom layer by atom layer in ultra-high vacuum.

name: Metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy
desc: Chemical vapour growth of compound semiconductor layers for LEDs and lasers.

name: Gallium nitride
desc: Wide-bandgap semiconductor whose high-quality growth enabled blue LEDs.

name: Quantum dot
desc: Semiconductor nanocrystals whose colour is set by size.

name: Photonic crystal
desc: Periodic structures that control light much as crystals control electrons.

name: Metamaterial
desc: Engineered structures with properties absent in nature, such as negative refraction.

name: Topological insulator
desc: Materials insulating inside but conducting on their surface, protected by topology.

name: Perovskite solar cell
desc: Cheap halide perovskite absorbers whose efficiency rose rapidly to rival silicon.

name: Nanotechnology
desc: Engineering matter at the 1 to 100 nanometre scale.

name: Metal–organic framework
desc: Porous crystalline frameworks of metal nodes and organic linkers for gas storage and capture.

name: Ancient tin trade
wiki: Tin sources and trade in ancient times
desc: Long-distance trade moving scarce tin from Cornwall, Iberia and Central Asia to bronze makers.

name: Repoussé and chasing
desc: Hammering sheet metal from behind and in front to create relief decoration.

name: Granulation
desc: Decorating gold with tiny fused spheres, a hallmark of Sumerian and Etruscan jewelry.

name: Filigree
desc: Jewelry of fine twisted gold or silver wire soldered into lacelike patterns.

name: Pewter
desc: Tin-based alloy used for tableware and vessels from ancient Egypt to the 19th century.

name: Lacquer
desc: Hard protective coating from the sap of the lacquer tree, used in East Asia since the Jomon period.

name: Lustreware
desc: Pottery with a metallic sheen from silver and copper nanoparticles in the glaze, from Abbasid Iraq.

name: Bone china
desc: English porcelain containing bone ash, strong and white, perfected by Spode around 1800.

name: Jasperware
desc: Wedgwood's unglazed coloured stoneware, a product of systematic ceramic experiments.

name: Stained glass
desc: Coloured glass pieces set in lead cames, used for church windows from the early Middle Ages.

name: Silvered glass mirror
desc: Chemical deposition of silver onto glass, replacing toxic tin-mercury mirrors.

name: Automatic bottle machine
desc: Owens's fully automatic glass bottle machine, which ended hand-blown bottle making.

name: Fused quartz
desc: Pure silica glass with very low thermal expansion and high UV transparency.

name: Bioactive glass
desc: Hench's glass that bonds to bone, the first bioactive material.

name: Case-hardening
desc: Adding carbon to the surface of iron to give it a hard steel skin.

name: Forge welding
desc: Joining iron pieces by heating and hammering them together.

name: Malleable iron
desc: Cast iron made ductile by long annealing, described by Réaumur.

name: Babbitt metal
desc: Tin- or lead-based bearing alloy that made high-speed machinery bearings practical.

name: Invar
desc: Guillaume's nickel-iron alloy with almost no thermal expansion, for precision instruments.

name: Monel
desc: Corrosion-resistant nickel-copper alloy used in marine and chemical equipment.

name: Nichrome
desc: Marsh's nickel-chromium resistance alloy, enabling electric heaters and toasters.

name: Stellite
desc: Haynes's hard, wear-resistant cobalt-chromium alloy.

name: Permalloy
desc: Nickel-iron alloy of very high magnetic permeability, used to load submarine cables.

name: Weathering steel
desc: Cor-Ten steel forming a stable rust layer that removes the need for paint.

name: Electroslag remelting
desc: Refining steel and superalloy ingots by remelting through molten slag.

name: Maraging steel
desc: Ultra-high-strength nickel steel hardened by precipitation rather than carbon.

name: Advanced high-strength steel
desc: Multiphase steels letting car bodies be lighter while staying crashworthy.

name: Cathodic protection
desc: Davy's method of stopping corrosion by making a metal the cathode of a cell.

name: Mond process
desc: Purifying nickel via volatile nickel carbonyl.

name: Anodizing
desc: Growing a protective oxide layer on aluminium electrochemically.

name: Crystal bar process
desc: Iodide process yielding ultrapure titanium and zirconium.

name: Zircaloy
desc: Zirconium alloy cladding for nuclear fuel, nearly transparent to neutrons.

name: Ferrite magnet
desc: Cheap ceramic iron-oxide magnets and cores used in motors and electronics.

name: Aluminium–lithium alloy
desc: Lighter, stiffer aluminium alloys for aircraft and rocket tanks.

name: Metal foam
desc: Cellular metals that are light and absorb impact energy.

name: Ferrofluid
desc: Colloid of magnetic nanoparticles in a liquid, developed at NASA.

name: Bismuth telluride
desc: Thermoelectric semiconductor used in Peltier coolers and generators.

name: Quasicrystal
desc: Shechtman's ordered but non-periodic crystals, overturning crystallography's rules.

name: Birkeland–Eyde process
desc: Electric-arc fixation of atmospheric nitrogen, superseded by Haber–Bosch.

name: Tetraethyllead
desc: Anti-knock gasoline additive that raised engine compression, later banned for lead poisoning.

name: PETN
desc: Powerful explosive used in detonating cord and boosters.

name: Ebonite
desc: Hard rubber made by heavy vulcanization, an early moulded insulating material.

name: Galalith
desc: Casein-formaldehyde plastic used for buttons and jewelry.

name: Cellulose acetate
desc: Less flammable cellulose plastic used for safety film and fibres.

name: Polyvinylidene chloride
desc: Saran, a barrier plastic used for food wrap and coatings.

name: Acrylic paint
desc: Fast-drying paint with acrylic polymer binder.

name: Ion-exchange resin
desc: Synthetic resins exchanging ions, used for water softening and rare-earth separation.

name: Melamine resin
desc: Hard thermoset used in laminates such as Formica and tableware.

name: Butyl rubber
desc: Gas-tight synthetic rubber used in inner tubes and tyre liners.

name: Cyanoacrylate
desc: Instant-setting superglue discovered by Coover.

name: Spandex
desc: Highly elastic segmented polyurethane fibre.

name: Hydrogel
desc: Water-swollen polymer networks, first used by Wichterle for soft contact lenses.

name: Hydrocracking
desc: Cracking with hydrogen over catalyst to make diesel and jet fuel.

name: Nomex
desc: Flame-resistant meta-aramid fibre.

name: Nafion
desc: Sulfonated fluoropolymer membrane used in fuel cells and chlor-alkali cells.

name: Kapton
desc: DuPont's heat-resistant polyimide film, used in flexible circuits and spacecraft.

name: Superabsorbent polymer
desc: Polymers absorbing hundreds of times their weight in water, used in diapers.

name: PEEK
desc: High-performance thermoplastic for aerospace and medical implants.

name: Metallocene catalyst
desc: Single-site metallocene catalysts giving precise control of polyolefins.

name: Shape-memory polymer
desc: Polymers that recover a programmed shape when heated.

name: Self-healing material
desc: Materials that repair damage on their own, such as White's microcapsule epoxy.

name: Cubic boron nitride
desc: Second-hardest material, used to machine hardened steels.

name: Niobium–tin
desc: Nb3Sn superconductor able to carry high currents in strong magnetic fields.

name: Magnesium diboride
desc: Simple, cheap superconductor at 39 K.

name: Amorphous silicon
desc: Non-crystalline silicon that could be doped, used in thin-film transistors and solar cells.

name: Atomic layer deposition
desc: Growing films one atomic layer at a time by alternating surface reactions.

name: Colloidal gold
desc: Faraday's ruby gold sols, the first studied nanoparticles.

name: Nanocellulose
desc: Cellulose fibrils and crystals at the nanoscale, strong and renewable.

name: DNA nanotechnology
desc: Seeman's use of DNA as a building material for nanoscale structures.

name: MXenes
desc: Two-dimensional transition-metal carbides and nitrides made by etching MAX phases.
